analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans fill prescriptions from pharmacies in countries with U.S.-comparable drug safety standards.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law generally bans importing prescription drugs from other countries, even the same medicines sold cheaper abroad, unless the drugmaker itself does the importing. This bill would have let individuals bring in up to a 90-day personal supply of a prescription drug from countries the FDA certifies as having safety standards at least as strict as America's, including Canada, Australia, Japan, and European Union members. The goal was to let Americans buy brand-name medicines at the lower prices those countries negotiate. It never moved past its first committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay U.S. retail prices for prescription drugs, especially people without generous insurance who buy brand-name medicines that cost far less in Canada and Europe. People could comparison-shop across borders for a 90-day supply with a valid prescription filled by a licensed pharmacist.

how_it_helps.text: Allows individuals to import or reimport a personal 90-day supply of a prescription drug, shipped directly to the consumer, filled by a licensed pharmacist, and accompanied by a valid prescription.

Limits eligible countries to a list — Australia, Canada, Israel, Japan, New Zealand, Switzerland, South Africa, EU member states, and European Economic Area countries — but only where the FDA certifies safety and effectiveness standards at least as protective as U.S. standards.
Excludes controlled substances, keeping the personal-import channel away from narcotics and other regulated drugs.
The bill's stated purpose is 'to reduce prescription drug costs by allowing the importation and reimportation of certain drugs.'

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose ability to charge U.S. patients prices far above what the same drugs sell for abroad depends on the import ban. U.S. pharmacies could also lose some fill volume to foreign sellers.

drawbacks.text: Safety risk is the standard objection: foreign supply chains can be harder to verify, and critics of importation argue consumers may receive counterfeit, expired, or improperly stored medicine. The bill tries to manage this by restricting imports to FDA-certified countries, licensed pharmacists, and documented prescriptions, but certification of a country is not the same as verification of every package.

The relief is narrow: it covers only personal 90-day supplies for individual consumers, so it does not lower prices for people who get drugs through insurance, Medicare, or hospitals, and it does nothing about the underlying U.S. pricing system.

Heavy personal importing could tighten supply in smaller countries like Canada, whose drug markets are much smaller than the U.S. market's — a concern those countries have raised about U.S. importation proposals generally.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who pay cash for expensive brand-name drugs, access to lower foreign prices would be a real, immediate saving. The safety safeguards are reasonable but not airtight, and the bill is a workaround rather than a fix — it leaves the pricing system that makes U.S. drugs the world's most expensive fully intact. Still, the cost side falls mainly on drug manufacturers, and the safety risk is manageable with the certification scheme the bill sets up.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, sent to the Health Subcommittee the next day, and never went any further before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the bill on December 12, 2013, joined by Rep. Dana Rohrabacher, a Republican, making it a bipartisan introduction.
It had 2 cosponsors, one Republican and one Democrat.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on December 12, 2013, and to the Subcommittee on Health on December 13, 2013.
No further action was taken; the bill died in committee when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers keep the import ban that lets them charge U.S. patients more than the same drugs sell for abroad. Consumers gain nothing.

for.name: Keith Ellison
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to allow personal drug importation from FDA-certified countries.

for.name: Dana Rohrabacher
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Fred Upton (R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled it for subcommittee or full-committee action, and the House never voted on it.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers (PhRMA and its members)
against.what_they_did: Long-standing, well-documented opposition to drug importation legislation on safety and pricing grounds.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat with a Republican as original cosponsor, but it drew only 2 cosponsors total and never reached a vote, so no partisan breakdown exists.

industries.note: U.S. law lets these companies charge American patients far more than the same drugs sell for in Canada and Europe, and the import ban is what keeps patients from shopping around. This bill would have opened a legal personal-supply channel around that pricing power.

industries.industry: Canadian and other foreign online pharmacies
industries.note: The bill would have let licensed pharmacists in certified countries ship prescription drugs directly to U.S. consumers, a new customer base at lower prices than U.S. retail. Their gain would come out of drugmaker U.S. revenue, not out of patients' pockets.
Some prescription volume could shift to foreign pharmacies, though the 90-day personal-supply limit keeps routine fills mostly domestic, and pharmacies themselves could use the import channel.
